bp: Short-video platforms are not only entertainment feeds. They are live public spaces where jokes, challenges, scams, harassment styles, unsafe acts, political messages, and coded references can appear, mutate, and spread before a policy team has a settled name for them. Moderation teams usually rely on annotation policies: written instructions that tell reviewers what issue a video belongs to and how to label it. The problem in this paper begins when the world moves faster than those instructions. A new content issue may not match any existing rule, so reviewers either miss it, label it inconsistently, or wait for humans to notice a pattern and rewrite the policy. The paper serves the practical system behind content governance: find unfamiliar clusters of problematic short videos early, describe what makes each cluster an issue, and turn that description into updated labeling policy before the trend has already reached many viewers.
wh: The hard part is that the platform is chasing a moving target. Existing rules are good at known problems, but emerging issues are defined precisely by not fitting the old list. A single video may look ambiguous: the visual scene, spoken words, captions, music, comments, and platform trend context may each carry only a small clue. Human discovery is careful but slow because people must notice repeated cases, compare them, decide whether they form a new issue rather than a variant of an old one, and then write policy language clear enough for future annotation. A purely rule-based system breaks because it can only search for issue shapes already named in the rule book. A simple classifier breaks for the same reason: it has learned past labels, while the operational need is to discover labels that are missing. The central tension is speed versus trustworthy policy formation.
naive: A smart beginner would start by expanding the current moderation rule list: add more keywords, suspicious visual patterns, and examples from recent violations, then ask reviewers to flag anything that seems unusual. That helps for known issues, but it fails at the boundary where new issues first appear. New trends often use new slang, reused sounds, visual templates, or coded behavior that was not in the rule list. Reviewers may also see isolated videos rather than enough related examples to recognize a pattern. Another beginner move is to sample popular videos manually every day. That is too slow and expensive, and it delays policy updates until after the trend has already spread.
ap: The paper's central move is to treat emerging moderation policy as a discovery problem before it is a classification problem. Instead of asking only whether each video matches an existing policy, the system first recalls short videos that may contain new issues. It then groups the recalled videos through a two-stage clustering process, where a cluster is meant to represent one newly discovered issue. The multimodal LLM agent is used as a worker that can read several kinds of evidence from a short video and help turn grouped examples into written annotation policy. In concrete terms, the system builds a loop: collect suspicious candidates, organize similar candidates into issue-shaped piles, summarize what each pile has in common, and generate policy updates that extend reviewer coverage. The abstract's strongest claim is operational: this loop was deployed and reduced both discovery delay and later exposure to problematic videos.
mech: The mechanism starts with the platform's incoming short videos and the current set of annotation policies. The first step is recall: the agent looks for videos that might contain potential new issues, meaning cases that deserve attention even if they do not cleanly match an existing policy. The abstract does not specify the exact recall signals, so the safe inference is only that the agent uses multiple media channels available in short videos rather than text alone. The second step is coarse grouping. Videos that appear to share an issue are placed near one another, so the system can stop treating them as isolated oddities. The third step is a second clustering pass, which refines the groups so that each final cluster corresponds to a distinct newly discovered issue rather than a loose mixture of several trends. After grouping, the agent examines each cluster as evidence: what repeated visual, audio, textual, or behavioral pattern makes these videos governable as one policy case? It then generates updated annotation policies from the cluster descriptions. Those policies flow back into the moderation process, giving future reviewers or downstream systems better coverage. The output is not merely a label on old videos; it is a changed rule set that can govern future videos faster.
math: The main mathematical idea is similarity-based grouping under uncertainty. Similarity here means deciding which videos are alike in the way that matters for governance, not merely alike in color, music, topic, or popularity. Each short video is a rich object with several channels. The system must compress those channels into comparable evidence, then ask which videos belong in the same neighborhood. Clustering is the operation of forming piles without already knowing the pile names. That fits emerging-issue discovery because the missing object is the new label itself: if the label already existed, ordinary classification would be enough. The two-stage strategy reflects a common tradeoff. A broad first pass can catch more possible issue videos but may mix different problems together. A refining second pass can separate the broad pile into cleaner issue groups. There is also a ranking or selection idea in the recall stage: because the platform cannot inspect every video equally, it must choose candidates likely enough to be worth clustering. The LLM agent adds language-and-media interpretation, turning grouped examples into policy text. The risk is compression: if the comparison map preserves decorative similarities while losing the harmful or policy-relevant clue, the clusters will look coherent for the wrong reason.
dots: Inside the repo's conference map, this paper sits between LLM agents, multimodal vision-language systems, misinformation and trust, and anomaly discovery. It resembles Smart Eye in the same batch because both use LLMs as practical proposal engines for deployed detection work, while still needing a more controlled downstream step to make the result auditable and efficient. It is also close to the cross-cultural hateful meme paper and the concept-grounded vaccine misinformation paper because all three moderation problems depend on meaning spread across images and language rather than a single text string. The deeper shared problem is evidence management for trust: find the small set of media examples that reveal a harmful pattern, explain why they belong together, and make the decision usable by a governance system. Compared with retrieval-augmented fake news detection, this paper does not retrieve outside evidence for one claim; it retrieves and groups platform examples to create a missing policy category.
ww: The method should improve over manual discovery because repeated weak clues become visible when the system groups many candidates together. One ambiguous video may not justify a policy update. Fifty related videos, sharing a visual template or behavior pattern, can reveal that the platform is facing a new issue rather than random noise. The agent helps because short videos are mixed-media objects: important meaning may sit in the relation between image, caption, audio, and trend form. A human policy team can reason about those relations, but not at the speed of a large platform. The two-stage clustering helps because discovery needs both breadth and precision. If recall is too narrow, new issues are missed. If grouping is too loose, the generated policy becomes vague and hard to apply. Refinement gives the system a chance to turn suspicious candidates into cleaner issue units. The reported deployment evidence supports this intuition: the abstract says emerging-issue discovery improved by more than 20 percent F1 and subsequent governance reduced problematic-video views by about 15 percent.
po: The payoff is faster policy iteration for a live short-video platform. Instead of waiting for human teams to discover a new issue, gather examples, and write updated rules from scratch, the system produces candidate issue clusters and draft annotation policies automatically. The abstract reports deployment in a real system, offline and online improvements in discovery, an F1 gain above 20 percent, and about a 15 percent reduction in views of problematic videos during later governance. Practically, that means the window between a harmful trend appearing and the platform having a rule for it becomes shorter.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The recall step must surface enough true emerging issues without drowning reviewers in ordinary videos. The clustering step must group by policy-relevant meaning, not by accidental features such as a popular sound or visual style. The agent-generated policies must be clear, stable, and reviewable by humans, because vague rules can create inconsistent or overbroad enforcement. The abstract reports strong deployed results, but it does not prove performance across every language, culture, adversarial trend, policy domain, or future platform change. It also does not specify how human oversight, appeals, false positives, or policy harms are handled.
